content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies continual graph learning. Targeting the problem that existing works assume a full access to historical data, during inference. This work proposes a model that does not store historical data and do not rely on complete neighborhood information. The proposed model has a encoder-decoder framework, so that graph data can be generated by the model to eliminate the necessity to store data. Experiments are done on 3 datasets with 4 baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. The motivation and the main ideas of the model is clearly explained and easy to follow.

2. The consideration that previous data may not be accessible is possible in certain real-world scenarios.

Weakness:

1. Although the idea that 'previous data may not be accessible' is intuitively correct, the authors actually do not provide any real-world examples on this. On the contrary, the datasets used in the experiments actually do not follow this assumption. For example, in citation networks like citeseer and cora used in this paper, the historical data is always available.

2. As for the potentially incomplete neighbourhod, if the neighbourhood information is incomplete or completely  unavailable during inference, then why would we use complete neighbourhood during training. There will be a concept drift if we do so. As an extreme case, the authors assume that sometimes only single nodes are given in inference. Then it seems that GNNs should not be used at all. What we should do is to train a simple single node classifier during training. Anyway, the reason we use GNNs is to use the neighborhood information for classification. If the the neighborhoood information is not available at all in inference, what is the point to use the in training? 


3. What is the size of the Amazon dataset and how many tasks are there in this dataset? The Cora and Citeseer are very small datasets with less than 10 classes, and are not enough for continual learning works. 

4. Only four baselines are compared, and one of them (GraphSAGE) is not continual learning method, which makes the comparison unfair.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity is good, 

Novelty is questionable, since the assumed scenario looks new but not justified with real-world examples. 

The quality is not enough, due to the questionable learning scenario assumed (mentioned in weakness), very small datasets, insifficient and unfair comparison with baselines. 

Not sure about the reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper assumes a intuitively possible learning scenario and proposes a model accordingly. But since the scenario is not justified with examples or in experiments, and the questionable experiments, I would recommend reject this paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors study continual graph learning without the assumption that the historical data can be  fullly accessed during the inference stage. To do this, they proposed Replay GNN (ReGNN). Experimental results are used to verify the effectiveness of their method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
They try to solve the case that the historical data are not available during inference in GNN, which is intesting. The experimental results demonstrate their effectiveness.

Weakness:
1) The two technical contributions with regard to corresponding challenges are largely separated. What is the intrinsic relationship between the modules corresponding to the two challenges?

2) Why it is challenging when the training graph is dense and testing graph is sparse. Whether it can be solved by simply sampling the neighbors in training graph?

3) It is hard to understand the Eq. (9). H_{N(v)}^{out} is equal to zeros?

4) In Figure 3, the training data consist of replay data generated by the graph encoder from the last task t − 1 and the current task. How to ensure catastrophic forgetting over previous tasks (e.g., k<t-1)?

5) The presentation needs to be improved, e.g., in the first paragraph of sec. 3.3.1, it confused me for those superscripts, making it hard to be understandable.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The novelty of this paper is limited, and the quality can be further improved.
content.summary_of_the_review: I incline to reject the paper due to the weakness mentioned above.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
Summary:

This paper studies continual learning settings in graph neural networks.

The author proposes a novel setting for continual earning in the graph learning scenario, where the historical data is not visible to the model during the inference, i.e. the graph neural networks cannot leverage connections stored in historical nodes for message passing.

The proposed setting is more realistic but has been overlooked by prior efforts.

The considered setting posts a new challenge, in addition to the original catastrophically forgetting problem.

To address these challenges, the author leverages two graph generative models to help augment the messages from historical data into the network.

Concretely, during the training phase, a GraphCAVE is trained to generate the missing data from previous tasks, and during the inference, a NodeVAE model is deployed to augment the missed neighborhood feature maps.

Empirical evaluations are conducted on Cora, CiteSeer, and AmazonCoBuyPhoto datasets, where the proposed method shows stronger performance over existing methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

- The proposed setting, i.e. historical data becomes invisible during inference, is closer to real-world applications. For example, companies would have wipeout policies with their data, i.e. if the user removes the data from their end, then the model forever loses access to that piece of data.
- Compared with the existing method, the proposed method takes this loss of information into the modeling and thereby enjoys strong empirical performance over existing continued learning under this new setting.
- Another point is that since the VAE models generate aggregated (averaged) features rather than embeddings for every single node, this method might introduce better privacy benefits if we consider Differentiable Privacy.

Weakness:

- The proposed method requires training T GraphCVAE and another NodeVAE module. It could pose an extra burden in optimization and training costs.
- Reproducibility: Perhaps I overlooked this, but I don't seem to find a reference to the code. The proposed method introduces several new modules, and there is certainly some complexity. Since there aren't enough references to the exact implementation details (and hyperparameters) of these modules, I would encourage the authors to consider releasing the code.

Question:

- Please correct me if I misunderstood, 1). The GraphCVAE only reconstructs node embedding rather than connectivity 2). Given an isolated node during the inference, the model relies solely on NodeVAE for prediction.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity and Quality:
I enjoy reading this paper; It presents with clear logic, proper intuitive explanations, and easy-to-understand visualizations.

Novelty:
The proposed setting is novel. While using generative models to avoid catastrophically forgetting is not a new technique, the NodeVAE module seems novel and relevant to the proposed setting.

Reproducibility:
Please see weakness 2.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I appreciate the new setting introduced by this paper, which I think is more realistic in practice. The proposed method is an interesting attempt to address new challenges and enjoys solid empirical performance. I would encourage the authors to publish the code as well to stem future works.

content.title: Data-Free Continual Graph Learning
content.TL;DR: consider and study an important yet ignored case in existing continual graph learning works
content.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), which effectively learn from static graph-structured data become ineffective when directly applied to streaming data in a continual learning (CL) scenario. A few recent works study this so-called “catastrophic forgetting” problem in GNNs, where historical data are not available during the training stage. However, they make a strong assumption that full access of historical data is provided during the inference stage. This assumption could make the graph learning system impractical to deploy due to a number of reasons, such as limited storage, GDPR1 data retention policy, to name a few. In this work, we study continual graph learning without this strong assumption. Moreover, in practical continual learning, models are sometimes trained with accumulated batch data but required to do on-the-fly inference with a stream of test samples. In this case, without being re-inserted into previous training graphs for inference, streaming test nodes are often very sparsely connected. It makes the inference more difficult as the model is trained on a much more dense graph while required to infer on a sparse graph with insufficient neighborhood information. We propose a simple Replay GNN (ReGNN) to jointly solve the above two challenges without memory buffers (i.e., data-free): catastrophic forgetting and poor neighbour information during inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our model over baseline models, including competitive baselines with memory buffers.
